<bot> That sounds like a good idea... just make sure *before* you go the degraded-array route...<endOfText>
<human> ... that you boot in recovery mode (root user) and comment out the /home mount from /etc/fstab temporarily, because Ubuntu has a *problem* booting with degraded arrays<endOfText>
<bot> Once the array is successfully rebuilt on the new drives, re-enable /home<endOfText>
<human> so whilst /home is not mounted ensure you always start to recovery mode root user (or manually edit the kernel command-line in GRUB to add 'single' to get a root single-user shell<endOfText>
<bot> There's a kernel problem with rebuilding degraded disks that boot relies upon... if mdadm gets a failed array message things get stuck<endOfText>
<human> Yes... or as I said, by editing the kernel command-line to use 'single'<endOfText>
<bot> there is a better way of course<endOfText>
<human> because the drives haven't failed... remove one drive from the array at a time using mdadm so the array has fewer members but is always a good array, swap drives, add the new drive to the array using mdadm and so on<endOfText>
<bot> Basically, if you can avoid creating a failed array you'll be better off<endOfText>
<human> is it a mirror or something else?<endOfText>
<bot> whatever RAID level is... you can only remove drives to take it down to the minimum required for that level, if you want to avoid a degraded RAID boot hang<endOfText>

<bot> well, for a three button mouse, for example, they represent which button to map to which function. so 1 2 3 would be the standard way, 3 2 1 the opposite (left and right reversed), 1 0 3 would be normal but with the middle button disabled. so you want to put a 0 in the position of the button you think is the one you want to disable. i.e. if you think it's the sixth button, do 1 2 3 4 5 0 7<endOfText>
